title: Individually Addressed Logical Pauli Measurements by QLDPC Surgery on a Trapped Ion Quantum Computer
abstract: Quantum low-density parity check (QLDPC) codes may lead to order-of-magnitude reductions in the qubit overhead required for fault-tolerant quantum computation. Achieving this improved overhead requires logical operations that selectively address individual logical qubits encoded within multi-qubit code blocks. Recently proposed architectures achieve this through QLDPC surgery, in which non-destructive Pauli measurements are performed using ancillary ''gadget'' systems transiently entangled with the code block, generalising lattice surgery. Here we implement QLDPC surgery on a [[10,2,3]] generalised bicycle code using Quantinuum's H2-2 trapped ion processor. A single-round surgery measurement using seven gadget qubits measures the $\bar{X}_1$ operator with a 0.72 [0.32, 1.41]% (95% credible interval) error rate and agrees with subsequent transversal measurement with 1.03 [0.60, 1.65]% error. Decoding across three rounds of syndrome extraction suppresses the gadget measurement error, reducing the error rate to below 0.26%. The syndrome after surgery confirms return to the code space and the unaddressed ''spectator'' qubit is preserved with error 0.21 [0.04, 0.67]% during the three-round measurement. We further demonstrate composition of conjugate basis gadgets by sequentially measuring $\bar{X}_1$ then $\bar{Z}_2$, reusing the gadget qubits, and obtain a 1.12 [0.60, 1.94]% error in the $\bar{Z}_2$ measurement. These results constitute a hardware validation of the generalised surgery primitive underlying Pauli-based computing for QLDPC architectures.
summary: This paper demonstrates the implementation of QLDPC surgery, a technique allowing for individual logical Pauli measurements within a multi-qubit code block, on a trapped ion quantum computer. By using ancillary 'gadget' qubits, the authors successfully suppress measurement errors over multiple syndrome extraction rounds. This work provides critical hardware validation for the generalized surgery primitive required for scaling fault-tolerant quantum computation using QLDPC codes.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of performing selective, individual logical Pauli measurements within the highly entangled structure of QLDPC codes to enable fault-tolerant quantum computation.
main_result: The authors successfully demonstrated the generalized QLDPC surgery primitive on a trapped ion quantum computer, achieving error rates below 0.26% after syndrome extraction, validating the approach for Pauli-based computing.
method: The core method involves implementing QLDPC surgery, which uses ancillary 'gadget' systems transiently entangled with the code block to perform non-destructive Pauli measurements.
model_or_system: The experiment is performed on a trapped ion quantum computer using Quantinuum’s H2-2 processor, implementing measurements on a specific $[[10,2,3]]$ generalized bicycle code.
key_observables: Error rates for single-round and three-round syndrome extraction (e.g., $ ar{X}_1$ measurement error rate of 0.72% initially, suppressed to <0.26%), and spectator qubit preservation error.
important_parameters: The code used is a $[[10,2,3]]$ generalized bicycle code; the process involves multiple rounds ($R=3$) of syndrome extraction to suppress errors.
main_assumptions: The primary assumptions relate to the connectivity defined by the Tanner graph for surgery and the error model, which may not fully account for measurement cross-talk.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the structure of the code and the merging of the measurement gadget with the code block, showing the support of the gadget components ($\kappa, \chi, \gamma$).
paper_structure: The paper progresses by establishing the need for selective measurement, detailing the gadget construction for $ ar{X}_1$, presenting the hardware implementation on the trapped ion platform, and finally validating the primitive through single-round, three-round, and sequential two-gadget measurements.
why_interesting: This work provides a crucial hardware validation of a generalized primitive (QLDPC surgery) necessary for scaling quantum computation beyond current limitations, directly impacting the feasibility of fault-tolerant quantum algorithms.
